g.passage: When the looms of the Tbilisi weaving cooperative fall silent each evening, I set two chairs by the window, and Anushka begins unwinding the tangled yarn the weavers leave behind. We used to play here for them on Fridays; now nobody asks. IRENA: You could leave the yarn tonight. ANUSHKA: (without looking up) And give up the only thing we still do on time? Later, when I reach for my violin case, she slides the spool toward me first, as she always does, so that I hold one end while she winds. Neither of us mentions the concert hall that cancelled our booking. IRENA: Same tempo as yesterday? ANUSHKA: Slower. Your hands are tired. g.passage: By the winter of 1994, Joon had conducted the Busan youth orchestra for eleven years, and every Thursday he still sat in the same barbershop chair beside Jakub, its youngest violinist. That afternoon Joon paid for both haircuts before Jakub could reach his wallet, then busied himself with a newspaper. Jakub, for his part, folded the receipt carefully into his coat rather than throwing it away. Later, at rehearsal, Joon gave him the solo that had always gone to the concertmaster, and no one in the hall questioned it. g.passage: Brass gears ticked on every wall of Tatiana's clock shop in Riga, where an old rule held that no clock could be sold until it had run a full year without losing a minute. Everyone obeyed it, though customers grumbled and many fine clocks were melted down for a single lost minute. On the morning Jakub was to leave for university, he found his mother lifting down the small clock he had built at twelve, which had once lost four minutes in a single winter. Keep it, she said, pressing it into his bag. A year is too long to wait for some things. Jakub said nothing, but at the station he wound it carefully and set it to her time. g.passage: When Zofia climbed to the roof that last evening in Thessaloniki, her father was already kneeling beside the water tank, a tin of sealant open at his knee. Eda, from the next roof, used to joke that the stain was older than Zofia's English. Zofia had stopped noticing it, the way she had stopped noticing that he never asked about the school prize ceremony he had missed. Now he pressed the sealant into the seam with his thumb and said, in Greek, that he should have done this long ago. g.passage: Tehran's southern road ended where the salt flat began, and it was there my aunt took me the morning after the wedding supper. I had salted the lamb twice; I knew it the moment Bahram, our guest of honor, praised the dish and reached for his water. My aunt had tasted it too, I was certain, for her mouth tightened, yet she said nothing at table and nothing on the long drive. On the flat she bent, broke off a plate of white crust, and showed me the dark earth kept moist beneath it. Salt covers, Shirin, she said; it also keeps. I did not understand her then. I only watched her wrap the shard in her handkerchief, as carefully as she folded our best linen, and carry it home in her sleeve. The wind lifted a fine white dust across the plain, erasing our footprints behind us.

Nothing has changed, I tell the surveyor.

We speak of walls, of tiles, of wells to dig,

g.passage: What does one do with hours that will not move? I asked myself this in the cabin above Bologna, where snow had closed the road for three days and the telegram from the hospital could not reach us. My old teacher, Moshe, spent the mornings mending a lamp whose wick had long since burned away. He trimmed a new one from a strip of his shirt, filled the reservoir, polished the glass, and then set it, unlit, on the sill facing the valley. Not yet, Assunta, he said, when I offered him a match. Each evening he wiped the frost from that pane before any other. On the fourth day a boy on skis appeared at the bend of the road, and Moshe rose so quickly that his chair fell. g.passage: Although the old tale says an apprentice must mend nets for seven years before she sails, I had mended them for only three when Nasrin gave me one of my own.
